title: 1,500 Years on a Cliff — and the Poles Aren't Holding It Up | China Travel Expert
description:
Everyone who sees the Hanging Temple assumes those spindly wooden poles underneath are what keep it from falling. They don't.

The temple is socketed into a sheer cliff on Mount Heng in Shanxi, about 75 m above the ground, and has hung there for roughly 1,500 years (begun around 491 AD, late Northern Wei). Its real support is a set of oak crossbeams driven deep into holes chiseled in the rock — the main structure is hidden inside the bedrock, so the weight is carried sideways into the mountain. Most of the thin vertical poles you can see were added later and bear very little load.

🧭 Expert Tip: the cliff walkways and plank stairs are narrow and basically one-way — go right at opening, before the single-file queues build up.

大家都以为是下面那几根细木柱撑着悬空寺——其实不是。真正受力的是插进崖壁的横梁，重量横向传进山体，细柱多为后来加的装饰。
